plan.topic: 'GLP-1 supplements' vs GLP-1 medicines: what's the difference, and evidence-based ways to support your own GLP-1
plan.angle: Slide 1: 'Do GLP-1 supplements work like semaglutide or tirzepatide?' Slide 2: the medicines were tested in large RCTs (STEP-1, 68 wk; SURMOUNT-1, 72 wk; adults with obesity or overweight plus a condition, without diabetes). Slide 3: 'GLP-1' supplements aren't FDA-approved drugs and haven't been shown in large trials to match these results. Slides 4–6: protein, fibre, and vegetables or protein before carbs, each 'linked to a higher GLP-1 response after meals in small studies', each healthy habits, not replacements, with source tags. Include the kidney caveat and 'build fibre up gradually'. Slide 7: prescriber questions. Last slide: disclaimer plus prescriber line.
plan.working_title: GLP-1 Supplements vs GLP-1 Medicines: What's Actually Different?
plan.why: A rising consumer search with few careful explainers so far, and a list format people save. It's also the bold myth-buster slot. | fact-check: Safe, on-pillar myth-buster, but it needs tighter scope. (1) Supplements: say that products sold as 'GLP-1 supplements' are not FDA-approved drugs and have not been shown in large randomized trials to produce weight loss comparable to semaglutide or tirzepatide. Do NOT say they 'don't work' or 'are dangerous' without a source. Name no products or ingredients. (2) STEP-1 = adults with obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes, 68 wk. SURMOUNT-1 = the same population, without diabetes, 72 wk. (3) Food-habit evidence is mostly small, short meal-test studies, e.g. the food-order study by Shukla et al. in Diabetes Care 2015 was in about 11 people with type 2 diabetes. These show higher post-meal GLP-1 or lower glucose, not weight loss. Say 'linked to a higher GLP-1 response after meals in small studies', and state that the effect is far smaller than the medicines and does not replace them. Every tag must point to a primary source that says exactly that. (4) Keep the kidney caveat for protein and 'build fibre up gradually with fluids'. (5) Playbook: carousels reach 0–3. Consider rebuilding this as a Short ('Do GLP-1 supplements work like tirzepatide?').

social.instagram_caption:
Are "GLP-1 supplements" the same as semaglutide or tirzepatide? They haven't been shown in large randomized trials to match these medicines.

Swipe to see the difference.

• Semaglutide and tirzepatide are FDA-approved prescription drugs, tested in 68–72 week randomized trials (STEP-1, SURMOUNT-1) in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Most common side effects: nausea, diarrhea.
• "GLP-1 supplements" aren't FDA-approved drugs. Makers, not the FDA, are responsible for their safety and labeling before sale.
• Small, short studies linked protein-first meals, carbs-last meal order and prebiotic fibre to a higher GLP-1 response after meals. They didn't measure weight loss, and these habits don't replace the medicines. Have kidney disease? Check protein with your clinician first. Build fibre up gradually, with fluids, unless you've been told to limit them.

factcheck.summary: This carousel is accurate and safe to publish as written. I checked every number against the primary sources. STEP-1 (NEJM 2021): 1,306 on semaglutide 2.4 mg vs 655 on placebo, −14.9% vs −2.4% at 68 weeks, with nausea and diarrhea as the most common side effects. SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022): 2,539 people randomized 1:1:1:1, about 630 per arm (630 on 5 mg, 630 on 15 mg, 643 on placebo), −15.0% / −20.9% vs −3.1% at 72 weeks. The population and the "not head-to-head" caveat are correctly stated. Kuwata 2016 (Diabetologia): 12 people with type 2 diabetes and 10 healthy volunteers in a crossover study. Fish-first and meat-first both raised GLP-1 compared with rice-first, and meat-first raised it more, so "meat (and, less so, fish)" is fair. Shukla 2017 (BMJ Open DRC): 16 adults with type 2 diabetes. Eating carbs last gave higher GLP-1 (about 38% higher area under the curve) and lower glucose (53% lower). Cani 2009 (AJCN 90:1236-43): 10 healthy adults, 16 g/day of prebiotic or placebo for 2 weeks, with higher GLP-1 and PYY. The FDA page confirms that makers are responsible for safety and labeling before sale and that FDA doesn't approve supplements before they're sold. The page says it was last updated 10/01/2024, which matches. The framing is careful throughout: small studies, post-meal hormone measures rather than weight loss, and habits presented as no replacement for medicine. The kidney, fluids and "don't stop or change your medicines" caveats are there, and the last slide has both the disclaimer and the prescriber line. There's one minor wording issue, about how the Cani group sizes are described.

issues.claim: 16 g/day prebiotic powder for 2 weeks raised post-meal GLP-1 vs placebo (10 healthy adults)
issues.problem: The 10 adults were split between the prebiotic and placebo groups. As written, the slide suggests all 10 took the prebiotic. Our rule is to give group sizes, never a combined N that hides the split.
issues.fix: 16 g/day prebiotic powder for 2 weeks raised post-meal GLP-1 vs placebo (10 healthy adults in total, split between prebiotic and placebo)

issues.problem: Same point as slide 4. The wording is acceptable, but it could be read as 10 people in each group.
